About this citation

A sequence of speeches on eros, and the speaker matters more here than in most dialogues: the passage on the ladder of beauty is Diotima's, reported by Socrates.

#### About Plato

Plato (c. 428/427–348/347 BCE) was an Athenian of high birth, a devoted associate of Socrates, and the founder of the Academy.

### Interpretation

Diotima's definition in the Symposium (206a) turns love from a feeling into a structure of desire. Everyone wants good things; love, in the strict sense, is wanting the good to be one's own, and to be one's own always. That last word does the work: because mortals cannot possess anything forever, love seeks the nearest substitute — “giving birth in beauty,” in children, in works, in laws, in ideas — which is why the speech moves at once from love to creativity and immortality.

#### Why it matters

It explains why love is restless even when it has what it wants: possession now is not possession always. The definition also suggests a diagnostic for any attachment — what good do you want to be yours, and is this the way to make it last?

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Love is the desire for the perpetual possession…”?

“Love is the desire for the perpetual possession…” comes from Symposium, 206a (c. 385–370 BCE), attributed to Plato.

#### What does Plato mean by love?

Greek distinctions among eros, philia, and agape, Confucian relational ethics, and modern debates about romantic love keep the theme philosophically precise rather than merely sentimental. This passage enters that discussion through love, morality.
